newsitem.title: UK: British government bids for moral high ground.
newsitem.headline: British government bids for moral high ground.

text.p: The British government sought on Wednesday to seize the political and moral initiative in the run-up to a general election with a raft of bills designed to put criminals in jail for longer and tighten school discipline.

But even before Queen Elizabeth announced the legislative programme -- the last before an election no more than seven months away -- in a glittering parliamentary ceremony, the government faced a furious onslaught from the opposition.
"Do these bills meet the requirements of society at the present time?...I am bound to say, they don't," Labour party deputy leader John Prescott told a BBC radio interviewer.

Capitalising on a campaign for national moral regeneration launched this week by the widow of a headmaster knifed to death by a teenager at his school gates, the government has crafted its programme to put the emphasis on personal responsibility.
The programme announced by the Queen included 13 bills.

Key among them was a bill to ban almost all handguns, except low calibre guns used in target shooting, in the wake of the massacre of 16 children and their teacher by crazed gunman Thomas Hamilton in the Scottish town of Dunblane in March.

There was also a bill fixing automatic life sentences for anyone convicted of a series of sex or violent crimes, another designed to crack down on welfare fraud and moves to tighten school discipline and increase selection of pupils by schools.
Another bill is designed to improve measures to prevent Britain's coasts being polluted by merchant ships.

But the government was accused of producing a "stripped-down" programme designed to highlight differences with the opposition, particularly on law and order, rather than deal with pressing social problems.

Prescott criticised the government for keeping moves to clamp down on "stalkers" -- who obsessively harass and even harm their targets -- and another setting up a register of paedophiles out of the government's list of bills.
The government has said it is looking at other ways of introducing the two measures.

But Prescott said: "Why couldn't we have put the paedophile register we have been calling for, the matter of stalking, into those bills...They could have been in the bill, but they (the government) really simply want to get into partisan arguments."

Education Secretary Gillian Secretary dismissed Prescott's attacks, telling the same interviewer: "The Queen's Speech is including bills which pursue the themes which we have consistently brought forward during the last 16 to 17 years."

But the bill on handguns has already run into trouble, with both Labour and the minority Liberal Democrats warning they will oppose the measure and instead vote for a total ban on handguns as demanded by the relatives of the Dunblane victims.

Aides to Labour leader Tony Blair said he would attack the government's attempts to leap on the moral bandwagon, telling parliament on Wednesday that a "fractured society" could not be mended by a government which had overseen its breakdown.

The Conservative party has been in power for an unbroken 17 years and polls show a majority of voters see it as out of touch and ridden with corruption after a series of financial and sexual scandals involving junior ministers.
Labour, thoroughly overhauled by Blair who has dragged it to the political centre, has a huge lead in opinion polls.
